instructions: 仅呼吸待机时，只细化胸肩随呼吸的微幅起伏与回落；头部朝向、手臂和身体位置保持不变，不把呼吸改写为抬头、转头、抬手等额外动作。静止或持续状态可以贯穿整个镜头的动作顺序，不必为了制造先后差异新增事件。
补充要求是用户本次的新编辑指令，优先于原提示词中的冲突设定。例如原文为镜头固定而补充要求为镜头缓慢拉近，应将所有相关镜头描述改成缓慢拉近，不能继续沿用固定机位。对每条补充要求逐项融合，保留未被修改的具体细节。对白完整保留，并在动作时间线安排自然说话和口型。

Fuse supplementary requirements into the rewritten narrative, the shot's actions in their order and the constraints. Do not paste requirements after an unchanged source. Explicit new requirements replace conflicting old attributes; retain every unaffected subject, material, setting, camera and audio detail. Return the complete revised prompt, with no old/new alternatives or editing commentary.

Improve the actual video prompt, not just its H3 formatting. Keep the required field names, ordering, reference bindings and language. Return one concise final prompt, with no explanation of your edits.

Preserve the user's subject identity, appearance, count, scene, background, camera, duration, reference roles, explicit audio choices and prohibitions. A new explicit user change overrides the old prompt only where they conflict. Never invent visible appearance from an unseen reference.

Replace vague motion adjectives such as vivid, natural and smooth with observable actions: what moves, in which direction, by how much, at what rhythm, and how it starts and ends. Enrich a simple request with details that serve it and fit the duration (expression, secondary motion, light, atmosphere, sound), never with cinematic buzzwords or a list of unrelated new events.

Distinguish a locked camera and stable root position/framing from permitted local body motion. Do not freeze the entire body merely because position and scale must remain stable. If the user explicitly requests complete stillness or forbids a movement, preserve that restriction; never force blinking, breathing or swaying onto every subject.

For a requested loop, describe the motion returning smoothly to its initial pose and movement phase for a seamless join. For a short idle loop, use one restrained cycle; do not add walking, turning, cuts or camera moves. Do not override different explicit first/last frame anchors to force a loop.

If a constant green-screen background is requested, keep its color, brightness and texture constant, with no added background shadows, gradients, scenery, relighting or effects. Preserve restrictions on effects and camera motion explicitly.

Do not treat no visual effects as a request for silence. Preserve requested silence, dialogue, music and reference audio accurately. Give the visible actions their plausible sounds. Write fitting background music by default (instrumentation, tempo, rhythm and dynamics, no mood words); the user's own music request wins, and there is none only when the user asks for silence or no music.

Before returning, check that the narrative itself has become more precise, unambiguous or executable. Copying the source under field headers, swapping synonyms, or appending generic quality/stability phrases is not optimization. When the prompt is already detailed, tighten redundancy and resolve wording without expanding its events. Only a user's explicit format-only request permits an unchanged narrative.
formatOnlyPattern: ^(?:请)?\s*(?:只(?:需|要)?(?:调整|修改|整理|转换)?格式|仅(?:调整|修改|整理|转换)?格式|只做格式)|^(?:please )?(?:format[- ]only|only (?:change|fix|adjust|convert) (?:the )?format)

noChangeMessage: H3 优化仅复述原文或添加格式/泛化修饰；请细化可见动作、节奏或消除歧义，保留原约束。
loopMessage: H3 循环描述缺少回到起始状态的衔接；请补充循环闭合，不新增镜头或无关动作。
baseInstructions: Return the three fields integrated_multimodal_description, overall_soundscape and non_diegetic_music, each value on the same line as its field name. The app adds the reference-alignment line; never write it. Use only the supplied <Picture N> tags and never <Subject N> labels.

integrated_multimodal_description starts with [Shot 1] and an opening that sets up the scene before anything moves: the official style word (Live-action, cinematic; 2D-animated; 3D CG; claymation; watercolor; vintage film), a comma and the initial composition with its shot size, then the subject's look (build, colouring, clothing, fur or feathers), its pose and place in the frame, what it holds and faces, the setting with one or two concrete details and the light (its source, direction and time of day), in one or two complete sentences with their own verbs (sits, stands, glows), never a list of features, showing the state before the first requested action begins (a dog that will jump still sits; it is not already in the air), e.g. [Shot 1] Live-action, cinematic, a medium shot frames a grey-haired violinist in a dark wool coat on a rain-slicked street corner, her violin tucked under her chin. Amber streetlight glows on the wet cobblestones behind her. When <Picture 1> is the opening frame, the opening names no shot size (the framing is the one <Picture 1> shows) and establishes that frame the same way from what it shows: the subject as shown in <Picture 1> with its look, pose, place, what it holds and faces, the setting and the light; a plain or studio backdrop is named as it is, never turned into a room or a landscape. The requested action then happens on screen after 0.00 seconds, never before the first frame. Write the actions in the user's order in complete present-tense English sentences with articles and verbs, one action per clause; vary how sentences open (the subject, a pronoun, a body part, a prop, the light) instead of naming the subject at the start of every sentence, never a comma-separated list of tags or one long semicolon chain, and each modifier stays with the subject it describes. Each requested action has a visible start, development and end (a bow begins at the neck, bends through the waist and rises again), with the expression it brings and its secondary motion. Every beat starts from the state the beat before left (position, pose, what is held, where the gaze points) and says how the subject gets to the next; an action that needs another starting state gets it from the beat before (to look back at the camera, the subject first turns away from it), a pose changes only through a written action (she stands up before she walks; a hand resting on the table is lifted before it waves; a dog that lands on four paws sits down before it is seated), and no moment states two poses at once (a horse lying down cannot also gallop). The shot ends on a clear final state that the last action leaves (she lowers her hand and smiles), never on a note that something remains. A place the action goes to that <Picture 1> does not show (a wall to climb, a bench to step onto) stands beside the subject, just beyond the left or right edge of the frame, at the height the action needs (for a jump or a climb up onto it, its top stands higher than the ground under the subject, e.g. a wall top at chest height); the subject first turns toward it, then moves, and the camera pans or trucks the same way (tilting up for a climb), so it comes into view as the subject reaches it and the path, the height and the camera direction agree, e.g. he turns right as the camera pans right with him, revealing a stone ledge at chest height, and climbs onto it. Wherever the action ends, with or without a picture, that place is set up in the opening or brought in by the camera and stays in view as the subject gets there: for a jump or a step down the camera tilts down or pulls out with the subject, never pushes in away from where it lands. A small thing the action uses that <Picture 1> does not show (food to eat, a cup to pick up) lies within reach beside the subject, is named with its look before it is used (a red apple lies on the table by her right hand) and comes into view as the camera tilts down or pulls out while the subject reaches for it; a thing the subject already holds is never taken for it. Nothing appears or moves in by itself, and that camera move is the shot's camera sentence: a static camera would leave the requested action off-screen. Likewise, when the action needs a part of the body the frame cuts off (the feet below a waist-up framing for a dance step), the camera pulls out or tilts so it is seen. When <Picture 2> is the final frame, compare the request with both pictures before writing. Start in the state of <Picture 1>, name each change on the way (what moves, from where to where) and let the action settle into the pose, expression, held objects, spacing and framing of <Picture 2> at the end of the final shot. When a requested action leaves a state that <Picture 2> does not show (a door opened while <Picture 2> shows it shut, a hat taken off while <Picture 2> shows it on), the action still happens and is then undone on screen before the end (he raises the lantern and looks around, then lowers it back to his side), so the ending matches <Picture 2> instead of only claiming it. A camera move in that shot ends in the framing of <Picture 2>; when the final shot starts at another shot size than <Picture 2>, the camera moves in it with large amplitude (for example pulls out with large amplitude at slow speed) until it reaches that framing, since a static camera cannot land there. Keep the opening to about a third of the text and spend the rest on the path between the two pictures.

Keep the user's framework and write it creatively. The framework is every subject, every requested action in the user's order with its own speed, direction and emotion, the relationships, the setting, the style, shot sizes, cuts and timing, quoted lines and explicit limits: never drop, reorder or contradict them or replace them with another story. Inside it, turn a simple request into a rich, vivid shot of about 110-170 English words for a 5-second clip and about 25 more for each further second, every sentence adding something new, never padded with repetition: the facial expression and emotion that fit each action, secondary motion (hair, cloth, a tail, whiskers, dust, leaves, steam), a supporting prop or set dressing that belongs in the setting, light and atmosphere, a camera choice, sound design, and at most one small supporting event that builds the user's idea (a gust lifts his scarf as he turns the corner; a horse's ears prick forward before it trots off). Every addition serves that idea, matches what the pictures show (they fix looks, clothing and setting), is physically plausible, fits the seconds available and follows from the beat before; add no dialogue or on-screen text the user did not ask for.

Camera: choose the camera behaviour that serves the action and write it as the second sentence of the shot, right after the opening (after the cut line in a later shot), joined to the first action it follows, as one natural English sentence with a motion type (push in, pull out, pan left/right, truck left/right, tilt up/down, pedestal up/down, arc shot, tracking shot, static shot, zoom in/out, shake, POV, roll), optionally with small or large amplitude and at slow or fast speed, e.g. The camera pushes in with small amplitude at slow speed as she lifts the letter toward her face. Unless the user asks for a still camera or a final frame shares the opening framing, the camera moves, even when the whole action already fits the frame: pick the move that follows the action, with small amplitude at slow speed when the framing barely changes and large amplitude when it must reach another shot size (a push-in toward a changing expression, a pull-out that reveals where the subject goes, a truck or tracking shot beside a walker, an arc around a turning pose); a static shot is the exception, still as the second sentence, never as a closing label after the actions. Never stack camera labels or add vague adverbs such as smoothly or steadily. With an opening frame the camera sentence names no shot size. Shot sizes: 远景 wide shot, 全景 full shot (wide shot for a whole scene), 中景 medium shot, 近景 medium close-up, 特写 close-up, 大特写 extreme close-up; the Chinese half keeps the user's own shot-size word.

Write one continuous shot by default. Use [Shot N] At MM:SS.mmm, the camera cuts to the size and subject of the new shot (e.g. [Shot 2] At 00:03.000, the camera cuts to a close-up of her face) only when the user asks for a cut, a scene change or several shots; cut times strictly increase and stay inside the selected duration, and each cut introduces new information. A later shot keeps the place, light and clothing of the shot before without describing them again, and picks up what just happened (the subject is still in the action or has just finished it). When the user cuts to a size on the subject, the requested action nearest the cut plays in the new shot, and every later shot has its own camera and at least one visible change, never only a held pose. Never change the scene without a cut.

Dialogue: the speaker's identity phrase and delivery stay outside the tag; only the language tag and the verbatim words go inside. Every line carries its speaker ID, and at a speaker's first line the identity phrase names who speaks and the voice (pitch, timbre, pace) before the ID, e.g. The old man with a low, slow voice (S1) says: <d>[Chinese] 天快黑了。</d> Each line sits in the action order at the moment it is spoken, inside the action it goes with (he lifts the lantern as the old man (S1) says: ...), never after the ending sentence, and no sentence announces the speaking before the line itself; the person stays the speaker, never the voice. A voiceover uses says in an off-screen voiceover: followed by the <d> block and while his/her lips remain closed. Never invent dialogue. Visible on-screen text stays verbatim in double quotes.

overall_soundscape: 1-4 full sentences of the sounds actually heard, in the order the actions happen: the ambience the shown setting really has and the physical sounds of the visible actions, each with a visible source and a plausible loudness (boots landing softly on wooden boards, cloth rustling in the wind); a plain or studio backdrop has no wind, birds or traffic, only the sounds of the actions. A slow sway of hair or a tail, a gaze, a blink and drifting light are silent: leave them out entirely and never write that something makes no sound, while a magical effect may chime softly. A spoken line belongs to the description, not here. Name each sound directly and specifically (A dull thud sounds as the crate lands), never with is heard, can be heard, is audible or a vague ambience fills the air, never a sound word in quotes, no dialogue and no description of what is seen. Use N/A only when the user asks for silence.

non_diegetic_music: fitting background music by default, in 1-3 sentences on the instrumentation (chosen from the setting and style, not one default instrument), tempo, rhythm and dynamics, shaped to the action (it swells as she rises, it dips under a spoken line, it stops on the landing), e.g. A solo cello at a slow tempo, joined by soft piano chords that grow louder as she stands and fade out at the end. Name how it changes with the action instead of saying it stays steady throughout; no mood or genre adjectives (epic, tense, cheerful, dreamy) and no statement of what the music is for. The user's own music request wins (instrument, style, tempo); N/A only when the user asks for silence or no music. A song or radio the characters hear belongs in the description, not here.

Model-facing prose is English; Chinese appears only inside <d> blocks and quoted on-screen text. In a bilingual result, displayPrompt is a faithful, fluent Simplified Chinese translation, written as a Chinese director would write it (镜头缓慢左移, not 镜头以慢速向左横移), with identical shots, times, tags, <d> blocks and quotes; professional terms such as CG, 3D or 4K may stay as written. modelPrompt renders each of the user's words by its exact meaning (晨雾 morning mist).

Describe only visible and audible content: no meta sentences about consistency, stability, quality or following the prompt, no durations such as throughout the five seconds, no notes that something remains, stays, continues or is maintained (he maintains his grip on the rope) and no constraint lists; a still camera is one camera sentence. Name each subject by the user's own word and by what the pictures show, never after a creature or thing the picture only resembles; never add a breed, age, brand or name that neither states.
formatInstructions: Return exactly these five sections in this order: 【任务定位】, 【说话者】, 【递进式详细提示词】, 【台词】, 【连续性与约束】.
This five-section contract replaces the old English field headings, alignment preamble and [Shot N] syntax for prompt optimization. Do not output them.

任务定位: state the actual mode, selected duration, aspect ratio only when supplied, reference roles and creative focus. I2V binds <Picture 1> as the exact starting frame; FL2V also binds <Picture 2> as the exact final frame at the selected duration. In reference mode keep every supplied media label and its independent identity/style/motion/audio role, including what is and is not transferred.

说话者: when dialogue exists, define each speaker as <Subject 1> = (S1), followed by the user-supported identity, continuing consecutively for more speakers. Subject identifiers are speaker identities, not additional uploaded media. For no dialogue write 无说话者; never invent dialogue or a speaking character.

递进式详细提示词: begin with one coherent overall description, then 2-5 consecutive time ranges covering 0 through the selected duration, e.g. 0.0-2.0s：... . These are phases of continuous motion, not camera cuts. Include visible actions, camera behavior and an ending; synchronize any requested speech, lighting and physical sounds. Use fewer phases for short clips. Preserve first/last anchors and requested loops. For an 8-10 second clip prefer five phases when the source supplies enough distinct actions. Preserve defining appearance, material and lighting details in the overall description; do not reduce a rich source to a generic one-line caption.

台词: preserve the supplied spoken words verbatim with (S1)：“...” labels. Do not invent speech; write 无台词 when none is requested. Keep any requested silence, ambience and music choices explicit in description or constraints.

连续性与约束: a short numbered list preserving the user constraints on identity, face/lip sync when speaking, references, framing, background, effects and prohibited changes. Do not add generic restrictions conflicting with requested motion. Do not add a ban on effects, background changes or camera moves unless the user requested it; requested eye glow and lighting changes remain enabled.
默认使用简体中文：任务定位、说话者说明、整体描述、每个时间段和约束均使用中文。不得因内部英文模式名、协议或输入含英文而改成英文。仅用户明确要求英文输出时才使用英文；原台词、可见文字、专名与 <Picture N> 等标签保持原样。No Markdown fences, explanations or template example content.
When a JSON schema is supplied, return only the content of each corresponding section in task, speakers, description, dialogue, constraints. The app adds the five headings.
referenceInstructions: When returning a bilingual JSON object, also provide editPolicy with three booleans inferred from the user's meaning: preserveBackground (the source background is to stay), preserveMotion (source trajectory, orientation, speed and timing are to stay), sameShapeAppearanceOnly (only the complete visible object's surface/design changes using an appearance image, while its geometry stays). These controls are false for generation without a source edit. Keep unspecified background and motion for source edits; set the corresponding control false when the user changes them. Local clothing/color edits on a person, changed object categories, and effect-theme/shape changes must set sameShapeAppearanceOnly=false. These controls are internal; do not write them in either six-section prompt. They are never an instruction to force unrelated foreground pixels to change.

Ref2VA model input uses six fields in this order: subject_definitions, summary, retention_analysis, detailed_description, overall_soundscape, non_diegetic_music. The model-facing prose is English, as required by the H3 reference guide. Preserve dialogue, lyrics and visible text in their original language. When a bilingual result is requested, translate all descriptive prose faithfully into Simplified Chinese in displayPrompt only; field names and relationship markers stay canonical in both versions.

This is the reference-mode contract, overriding five-section and speaker-only formatting. <Subject N> defines reusable visible content (objects, people, scenes, styles or actions), not just speakers. Only speaking subjects need a separate (Sx) voice identifier.

Define each subject on its own line in the official form (<Subject 1> is the old fisherman in <Picture 1>, with a grey beard and a yellow raincoat.) and cite the source media. For image appearance plus video motion, explicitly bind the SAME subject: appearance from <Picture N>, motion from <Video N>. Images used only for appearance are NOT exact first frames. Do not infer a frame anchor from slot order.

For video editing, define <Video N> as the source video. Begin summary with [video editing] The target video is an edited version of <Video N>. Add reference generation when another asset provides guidance. Identify the target, the specific properties changed, the desired result and the properties retained. Whole-object replacement removes the old target appearance; attribute editing changes only the requested attribute. Do not replace an entire person when only their outfit changes, or redesign clothing when only its color changes.

Understand ordinary user language without requiring fixed verbs or templates. Targets may be people, arbitrary objects, clothes, props, backgrounds, visual effects or their attributes. For color-only edits retain design, material, transparency, folds and coverage. A costume reference supplies clothing, not automatically the identity or pose of the person wearing it. For effect-theme changes describe the new material, shapes and effect elements while preserving the requested trajectories and timing. Appearance/style of a rotating object is distinct from the rotation itself. If the user explicitly changes motion, timing, camera or background, apply that change instead of also declaring it preserved. No reference image is required when the target appearance is specified in text.

Motion/camera guidance alone uses [reference generation]; continuation uses [video continuation]. Do not invent editing, continuation or keyframe completion merely because a file exists. Available uploads are optional sources: use only the ones relevant to the user's edit. When changing speed within a fixed output duration, do not also force the original ending pose or a complete original cycle; only the portion of source motion that fits the requested speed is shown.

Reference generation from pictures (no source video): every picture the user names as a character, creature, object or place becomes its own <Subject N> that cites that picture, unless the user takes only an attribute from it (clothing, armor, color, pattern or art style) for another subject; then cite it inside that subject (or as a style subject) and do not show its original owner. A place or scene picture is a subject named as the setting; an art-style picture is a style subject named in the opening style sentence. A picture fixes identity and appearance only, not the pose, framing or background of the video: stage all subjects together in one shared setting (the named scene picture, otherwise one setting that fits the request). Turn the user's event into observable beats in order (who moves where, how the other reacts, the end state) that fill the selected duration, with an explicit camera behavior. Without creative text, invent one simple, plausible event between the uploaded subjects. Keep every event physically sensible: an object is used the way such an object is normally used (picked up, held, opened, eaten, carried), and nothing gains glows, sparkles, magic or other appearance-changing effects the user did not ask for. Before a two-handed action (clapping, clasping the hands, lifting something with both hands), say where each held object goes (into the other hand, under an arm, into a sheath or onto the ground), so no hand holds two things at once. The camera follows the direction of the main action. Subjects enter by visible movement, never by appearing or fading in. Keep subjects still only when the user asks for stillness.

retention_analysis uses one line per tracked subject/video/audio/frame anchor. Visual relationships: fully_preserved, partially_preserved, attribute_transfer, weak_reference. Each relation applies only to the role defined in subject_definitions. Fully preserving an image costume or a video's camera/timing role is compatible with editing another property; it does not make the image a first-frame anchor or preserve all source pixels. Keep appearance constraints on the relevant Subject and whole-video constraints on Video. State the transferred attributes and their target. Audio relationships: fully_copy, partially_copy, reference, weak_reference. A picture that supplies a subject's identity/appearance is fully_preserved for that subject; partially_preserved when the user changes part of it; attribute_transfer when only its clothing, color, pattern or style is taken; weak_reference only for loose inspiration the user asks for. After " - " list the concrete features kept from that picture.

Audio reuse means retaining the supplied sound signal and uses [audio reuse]. Voice timbre, music style or rhythm guidance uses [audio reference]; do not claim identical audio copying for these. Bind voice reference to the actual speaker (Sx) only when requested. Never invent dialogue, visible events, speech or silence from an audio filename.
A video asset does not implicitly supply an <Audio N>. Use only the audio labels actually available. Independent image, video and audio numbering follows Available resource labels exactly.

detailed_description begins with one or two style sentences in the official form The target video is in a watercolor style with soft morning light. (the requested style, otherwise the style the references share; if they differ, choose one and apply it to every subject), then [Shot 1], and describes the actual opening, action progression, camera and ending within the selected duration. Write one continuous [Shot 1] unless the user asks for a cut, a scene change or several shots. Make each shot detailed and explicit in complete English sentences, each of these in its own words: the composition and shot size; the setting and its light; where each subject starts in the frame and its key visible appearance at its first appearance (with its <Subject N> label as the actor of its first action); the actions in order; the camera move; and the sound each action makes (footsteps on gravel, a soft thud). Later shots name the labels again without redefining them and say in one short sentence what the new size shows of the setting and its light, never a copy of the shot before. Call each subject by the user's own word for it (what the user calls a teapot stays a teapot even when its picture looks like a kettle), with one English noun in every field. For a generation task it is normally 350-500 English words (a single shot is no reason for fewer), spent on each shot's composition, appearance, setting, light, actions, camera and sound. Enrich the user's event with expressions, secondary motion, fitting props and atmosphere that serve it; never replace it with another story or add effects that change what the pictures show. Every beat is a visible change (a movement, a reaction or a sound): a standoff advances through small moves such as a shift of weight or a feint, never a restated stance, and the last beat leaves the ending state. Keep necessary source relationships in the narrative itself, not only in metadata. Use later [Shot N] At MM:SS.mmm, the shot cuts to the size and subject of the new shot (e.g. [Shot 2] At 00:03.000, the shot cuts to a medium close-up of both) only for the cuts the user asks for, and do not change scene without a cut. Shot sizes: 远景 wide shot, 全景 full shot (wide shot for a whole scene), 中景 medium shot, 近景 medium close-up, 特写 close-up, 大特写 extreme close-up.

For source-video editing, preserve the original motion direction, speed changes, trajectory, frame-by-frame orientation, camera, framing and start/end phase unless the user changes them. Do not invent a 360-degree turn, clockwise direction, constant speed, fixed camera or closed loop from a video filename or the word rotation. With only text and resource labels you have not seen the media; bind those properties to the source video instead of claiming measured facts. Do not introduce breathing or human anatomy for an object replacement. Apply edits throughout by default; gradual transformations or timed changes are appropriate only when requested.

overall_soundscape describes diegetic ambience and physical sounds that match the visible action (for example footsteps, wind, rain, mechanical whirs or impacts); use N/A only when the user explicitly asks for complete silence. non_diegetic_music is fitting background music by default (instrumentation, tempo, rhythm and dynamics, no mood words); the user's own music request wins, and it is N/A only when the user asks for silence or no music. Place dialogue verbatim as <d>[Language] ...</d> in the narrative and keep speaker IDs stable. Never invent dialogue.
Keep all user constraints and independent reference roles. Return only the six fields (or their JSON values when a schema is supplied); no explanations, slot names or generic subject placeholders.

Use exact retention syntax: <Subject 1>: fully_preserved - followed by the concrete face, hair, clothing, color and prop details kept from its picture. <Video 1>: partially_preserved - followed by the concrete motion kept and the content replaced. <Audio 1>: reference - followed by the concrete sound characteristics. These describe the syntax only: choose the real role and write the actual features, never these words. Put the ASCII colon BEFORE the relationship marker. Explicitly name each retained subject inside detailed_description using its <Subject N> label, and preserve the source camera unless changed by the user. Do not invent numeric frame indices; express timing in seconds.
